doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Lean times around 1967-68 and day jobs before Lee Morgan's call
summary: Work was tight so he took a job at Alexander's, and each time he took a day job a gig, like Lee Morgan's, came.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Was there a period of, was there any particular period of time, a decade or whatever, that it got harder to make a living in the jazz world?

Oh well I can tell you precisely. I think, let me see now, it could have been around maybe close to ’68, ’67, ’68. Things were getting a little tight so I would always say well it’s no point in me waiting for the phone to ring so. So I said let me see what I can find. Now mind you playing music all my life I had no expertise in anything. I didn’t have any college degree, I didn’t know anything, auto mechanics, woodwork, no other skills. So I went to Alexander’s Department Store and got the job. And I had my shirt and tie on and I guess they called me an Expediter, whatever that means, “May I help you,” or, “How may I help you” and I worked that job, punched my clock, brought my little pay home. It wasn’t a lot of money. And the minute that happened, that’s when the phone rang and it was Lee Morgan, he said, “Hey man I’ve got this gig” wouldn’t you know. So anytime things got a little tight I’d go to the day job then a jazz job would come through. So then I got the job with Lee and I think before that I worked a place called Fleet Messenger Service. I think my pay was, after taxes, thirty-six dollars, can you believe that? After taxes.
